Two statements are given below
Statement I : In H atom, the energy of 2 s and 2 p orbitals is same
Statement II : In He atom, the energy of 2 s and 2 p orbitals is same

options: Both statements I and II are correct
Both statements I and II are not correct
Statement I is correct but statement II-is not correct
Statement I is not correct but statement II is correct
questions.solution:
The energy of the orbitals in hydrogen atom increases as follows: $1 \mathrm{~s} \lt 2 \mathrm{~s}=2 \mathrm{p} \lt 3 \mathrm{~s}=3 \mathrm{p}=3 \mathrm{~d} \lt 4 \mathrm{~s}=4 \mathrm{p}=4 \mathrm{~d}=4 \mathrm{f} \lt $
The energy of an electron in a multi electron atom, unlike that of the hydrogen atom, depends not only on its principle quantum number but also on its azimuthal quantum number. So only I statement is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The wavenumber of first spectral line of Lyman series of $\mathrm{He}^{+}$ion is $x \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$. What is the wavenumber (in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$ ) of second spectral line of Balmer series of $\mathrm{Li}^{2+}$ ion?
questions.solution:
For Lyman $\begin{aligned} & \overline{\mathrm{v}}=\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{H}} \times \mathrm{Z}^2\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}_1^2}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}_2^2}\right] \\ & =\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{H}} \times 2^2\left[\frac{1}{1^2}-\frac{1}{2^2}\right] \\ & =\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{H}} \times 4 \times \frac{3}{4} \\ & \overline{\mathrm{v}}=3 \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{H}}=\mathrm{x} \\ & \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{H}}=\frac{\mathrm{x}}{3}...(i) \end{aligned}$
For Balmer series $\begin{aligned} & \overline{\mathrm{v}}=\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{H}} \times 3^2 \times\left[\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{4^2}\right] \\ & =\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{H}} 9 \times \frac{3}{16}. \end{aligned}$
Putting the value of $R_H$ from eq. (i) $\bar{v}=\frac{x}{3} \times 9 \times \frac{3}{16}=\frac{9 x}{16}$

Assertion (A): First ionisation enthalpy of oxygen is less than that of nitrogen
Reason (R): Atoms with half-filled or completely filled orbitals are less stable
The correct option among the following is
options: (A) and (R) are true. (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
(A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution: The first ionisation enthalpy of oxygen is less than that of nitrogen. This is due to the stability of halffilled electronic configuration. Nitrogen has half filled electronic configuration and hence its ionisation energy is greater than oxygen. In oxygen, after losing its electron, it goes to half filled electronic configuration and hence, it has less ionisation energy than litrogen.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match the following
$List-I
(Complex)$
(A) $\left[\mathrm{CoF}_6\left[^{3-}\right.\right.$
(B) $\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4\right)_3\right]^{3-}$
(C) $\left[\mathrm{FF}_6\right]^{3-}$
(D) $\left[\mathrm{Mn}(\mathrm{CN})_6\right]^{3-}List-II
(Spin only Magnetic moment)$
(I) 0
(II) $\sqrt{24}$
(III) $\sqrt{8}$
(IV) $\sqrt{35}$
(V) $\sqrt{15}$
The correct answer is:
questions.solution:
$\left[\mathrm{CoF}_6\right]^{3-}: \mathrm{Co}$ is present as $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$ and $\mathrm{F}^{-}$is a weakfield ligand.
Thus, $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}=[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 \mathrm{~d}^6$ with four unpaired electrons.

\Rightarrow \mu=\sqrt{\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{n}+2)} \text { B.M. }=\sqrt{4(4+2)}=\sqrt{24}

$\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4\right)_3\right]^{3-}: \mathrm{Co}$ is present as $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$ and $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4{ }^{2-}$ is strong-field ligand.

Thus, $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}=[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 \mathrm{~d}^6$ with all paired electrons.

\mu=\sqrt{\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{n}+2)}=\sqrt{0(0+2)}=0

$\left[\mathrm{FeF}_6\right]^{3-}: \mathrm{Fe}$ is present as $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ and $\mathrm{F}^{-}$is a weak-field ligand.

Thus, $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}=[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 \mathrm{~d}^5$ with five unpaired electrons.

\Rightarrow \mu=-\sqrt{\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{n}+2)}=\sqrt{5(5+2)}=\sqrt{35}

$\left[\mathrm{Mn}(\mathrm{CN})_6\right]^{3-}: \mathrm{Mn}$ is present as $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}$ and $\mathrm{CN}^{-}$is a strongfield ligand with $\mathrm{CN}^{-}$pairing-up only two electrons. Thus, $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}=[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 \mathrm{~d}^4$ with two unpaired electrons.

\mu=\sqrt{\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{n}+2)}=\sqrt{2(2+2)}=\sqrt{8}

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The threshold frequency of a metal is $10^{15} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. The ratio of maximum kinetic energies of the photoelectrons, when the metal is made to strike with radiations of frequencies $1.5 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ and $2.0 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ respectively is
questions.solution:
$v_0=1.0 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$
Maximum kinetic energy will be at the highest frequencies and when all the energy is utilized for the kinetic energy of the ejected electrons:
$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E}_1=\mathrm{h}\left(v_1-v_0\right) \\
& =6.626 \times 10^{-34}\left(1.5 \times 10^{15}-1.0 \times 10^{15}\right) \\
& =6.626 \times 10^{-34}\left(0.5 \times 10^{15}\right) \\
& =3.313 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J} \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{K}_{.} \mathrm{E}_2=\mathrm{h}\left(v_2-v_0\right) \\
& =6.626 \times 10^{-34}\left(2.0 \times 10^{15}-1.0 \times 10^{15}\right) \\
& =6.626 \times 10^{-34}\left(1 \times 10^{15}\right) \\
& =6.626 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}$
Thus, the ratio will be :
$\frac{\mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E}_1}{\mathrm{~K} . \mathrm{E}_2}=\frac{3.313 \times 10^{-19}}{6.626 \times 10^{-19}}=1: 2$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The kinetic energy of electrons emitted, when radiation of frequency $1.0 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~Hz}$ hits a metal, is $2 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}$. What is the threshold frequency of the metal (in Hz)?
$\left(h=6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}\right)$
questions.solution:
Given : - Kinetic energy $=2 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}$
Radiation of frequency $=1.0 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~Hz}\mathrm{h}=6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}$
According to Einstein's equation
Kinetic energy $=1 / 2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{V}^2=\left(\mathrm{V}-\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{o}}\right) \qquad ...\mathrm{(1})\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{e}}=$ mass of electron
$\mathrm{V}=$ Frequency of incident radiation
$V_0=$ Threshold Frequency
Putting the value in equation (1)
$\begin{aligned}
& 2 \times 10^{-19}=6.62 \times 10^{-34}\left(1.0 \times 10^{15}-\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{o}}\right) \\
& \frac{2 \times 10^{-19}}{6.62 \times 10^{-34}}=1.0 \times 10^{15}-\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{o}} \\
& \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{o}}=1.0 \times 10^{15}-0.302 \times 10^{15} \\
& \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{o}}=0.698 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}=6.98 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The uncertainty in determination of position of a small ball of mass 10 g is $10^{-33} \mathrm{~m}$. With what $\%$ of accuracy its speed can be measured, if it has a speed of $52.5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ ?
$\left(h=6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}\right)$
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{x} \cdot \Delta \mathrm{p}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{4 \pi} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{x} \cdot \mathrm{m} \Delta \mathrm{v}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{4 \pi} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{v}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{4 \pi \cdot \Delta \mathrm{x} \cdot \mathrm{m}}=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{~J} . \mathrm{S}}{4 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-33} \mathrm{~m} \times 10 \mathrm{~g}} \\ & \Delta v=0.52 \times 10^{-34} \times 10^{33} \times 10^{-1} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^2 \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \times \mathrm{m}^{-1} \times \mathrm{g}^{-1} \\ & =0.52 \times 10^{-2} \times 10^3 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \times \mathrm{g}^{-1} \\ & =0.52 \times 10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \\ & 52.5 \times \frac{\mathrm{x}}{100}=0.52 \times 10\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & x=\frac{0.52 \times 1000}{52.5} \\ & x=9.9 \approx 10\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The uncertainties in the velocities of two particles $A$ and $B$ are 0.05 and $0.02 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ respectively. The mass of $B$ is five times to that of mass $A$. What is the ratio of uncertainties $\left(\frac{\Delta x_A}{\Delta x_B}\right)$ in their positions?
questions.solution:
According to Heisenberg
$\Delta x \times m \times \Delta v=\frac{h}{4 \pi}$
where $\Delta x=$ uncertainty in position.
$m=$ mass of particle
$\Delta v=$ uncertainty in velocity
According to question
$\Delta x_A \times m \times 0.05=\frac{h}{4 \pi}\ldots(1)\Delta x_B \times 5 m \times 0.02=\frac{h}{4 \pi}\ldots(2)$
Eq. (1) divided by Eq. (2), then
$\frac{\Delta x_A \times m \times 0.05}{\Delta x_B \times 5 m \times 0.02}=1$
or $\frac{\Delta x_A}{\Delta x_B}=2$

questions.q: An electron is moving in Bohr's fourth orbit. Its de-Broglie wave length is $\lambda$. What is the circumference of the fourth orbit?

According to Bohr's concept, an electron always move in the orbit with angular momentum ( $m v r)$ equal to $n h / 2 \pi$.
$\therefore \quad m v r=\frac{n h}{2 \pi}$
or
$r=\frac{n}{2 \pi} \cdot\left(\frac{h}{m v}\right) \text { or } r=\frac{n \lambda}{2 \pi}$
(From de -Broglie equation, $\lambda=\frac{h}{m v}$ )
for fourth orbit $n=4\begin{gathered}
r=\frac{2 \lambda}{\pi} \\
\therefore \text { circumference }=2 \pi r=2 \pi \times \frac{2 \lambda}{\pi}=4 \lambda
\end{gathered}$

questions.q: In a nuclide, one a.m.u. of mass is dissipated into energy to bind its nucleons. The energy equivalent of this mass is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & 1 \mathrm{amu}=1.492 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{erg} \\ & 1 \mathrm{MeV}=10^6 \times 1.602 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{erg} \\ & \therefore \quad 1 \mathrm{amu}=\frac{1.492 \times 10^{-3}}{1.602 \times 10^{-12} \times 10^6} \\ &=931.5 \mathrm{MeV} \\ & \therefore \quad 1 \mathrm{MeV}=10^6 \mathrm{eV} \\ & 1 \mathrm{amu}=931.5 \mathrm{MeV} \\ &=931.5 \times 10^6 \mathrm{eV}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: If the electron of a hydrogen atom is present in the first orbit, the total energy of the electron is
questions.solution:
Kinetic energy $=\frac{1}{2} m v^2$
Potential energy $=\frac{-e^2}{r}$
But $m v^2=\frac{e^2}{r}\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{e^2}{r}$
Total energy $=\mathrm{KE}+\mathrm{PE}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{e^2}{r}-\frac{e^2}{r}=\frac{e^2}{r}\left(\frac{1}{2}-1\right)=\frac{-e^2}{2 r}$

questions.q: If the mass defect of a nuclide is $3.32 \times 10^{-26} \mathrm{~g}$, its binding energy is $\mathrm{MeV}$
questions.solution:
Mass defect $=3.32 \times 10^{-26} \mathrm{~g}=\frac{3.32 \times 10^{-26}}{1.66 \times 10^{-24}} \mathrm{amu}$
Binding energy $=$ Mass defect $\times 931 \mathrm{MeV}=\frac{3.32 \times 10^{-26}}{1.66 \times 10^{-24}} \times 931=18.62 \mathrm{MeV}$
